name: SS-31
summary: A lab-made peptide that targets mitochondria, FDA-approved in 2025 as Forzinity for Barth syndrome and taken off-label for aging and energy based mostly on animal studies.
what_it_is: SS-31, or elamipretide, is a small synthetic peptide that binds cardiolipin, a fat in the inner membrane of mitochondria, the parts of cells that make energy; its label says this improves mitochondrial structure and function. FDA approved it in 2025 as Forzinity to improve muscle strength in Barth syndrome, a rare inherited mitochondrial disease. People also take it hoping to slow aging, based mainly on mouse studies.

evidence.why: FDA's accelerated approval rests on strength gains in about 10 people with Barth syndrome during an open-label extension, after a 12-week placebo-controlled phase in 12 patients missed its goals; a 218-person trial in mitochondrial myopathy found no benefit, and anti-aging effects come from mouse studies.

status_us.label: FDA-approved (Forzinity) for Barth syndrome only
status_us.note: FDA granted accelerated approval in September 2025 to improve muscle strength in people with Barth syndrome weighing at least 30 kg, after first declining the application in May 2025; continued approval may depend on a confirmatory trial. Use for aging, energy or any other condition is off-label.

benefits.claim: Gradual gains in knee muscle strength over months to years of open-label treatment in about 10 people with Barth syndrome, the basis for accelerated approval; strength did not improve during the 12-week placebo-controlled phase
Substantially reversed age-related problems with heart relaxation (diastolic dysfunction) and lowered mitochondrial oxidative stress in old mice after 8 weeks

risks.risk: Injection-site reactions in every treated patient in the Barth syndrome trial: redness, pain, hardening, itching, and sometimes bruising or hives
Serious allergic reactions needing emergency care have been reported, along with rashes and cough; they can begin minutes to months after starting
Higher eosinophil counts (a type of white blood cell) with longer use, peaking around 90 days and later returning to baseline
Drug levels rise when kidney function is reduced, and it has not been studied in people on dialysis
Safety for aging or wellness use has not been studied; in a 24-week trial in 218 adults with mitochondrial myopathy, side effects were mostly mild to moderate

avoid_if: Known serious allergy to elamipretide or its ingredients (contraindicated)
Newborns, especially premature babies (the product contains benzyl alcohol, which has caused fatal reactions in them)
Severe kidney disease or dialysis (drug levels rise; dialysis not studied)
interactions: In lab tests it blocks MATE1, a kidney transporter that clears some drugs; clinical studies found no meaningful effect on aspirin, clopidogrel or heparin

during: Complete blood count, since eosinophil counts often rose with longer use
labs.why: These follow the label's notes on kidney function and eosinophils; for off-label use in healthy people, no evidence-based monitoring exists.

studies.title: Efficacy and Safety of Elamipretide in Individuals With Primary Mitochondrial Myopathy: The MMPOWER-3 Randomized Clinical Trial
studies.people: 218 adults with genetically confirmed primary mitochondrial myopathy
studies.finding: After 24 weeks, elamipretide did not improve 6-minute walk distance or fatigue compared with placebo. It was well tolerated, with mostly mild to moderate side effects.

studies.title: FORZINITY (elamipretide) prescribing information (updated December 2025)
studies.people: 12 males aged 12 and older with Barth syndrome in a crossover trial; 10 continued in an open-label extension
studies.finding: The 12-week placebo-controlled phase missed its main goals (walking distance and fatigue), and strength did not rise. In the extension, median knee strength rose by week 12 and stayed higher through week 168, which FDA accepted for accelerated approval.

studies.title: Late-life restoration of mitochondrial function reverses cardiac dysfunction in old mice
studies.finding: Eight weeks of SS-31 substantially reversed diastolic dysfunction and lowered mitochondrial oxidative stress in the heart, similar to a gene therapy that boosts a mitochondrial antioxidant enzyme.

ask_your_clinician: What do human trials show for my goal, given that the approval covers only Barth syndrome?
How would we watch for allergic reactions and injection-site problems?
Does my kidney function affect whether this is safe for me?

notes_for_editor: Seed claim confirmed: the DailyMed label (updated December 10, 2025) shows initial US approval in 2025 under accelerated approval for Barth syndrome (patients weighing at least 30 kg). The September 19, 2025 date and the May 2025 complete response letter come from the company's press release (source 2), not an FDA document. Grade set to 'limited' rather than the 'approved drug = strong' rule, because the approval rests on an open-label extension in about 10 patients after the randomized phase missed its endpoints. Elamipretide is not on FDA's 503A nomination list (May 14, 2026) or its Category 2 page, and WADA's 2026 list does not name it. Heart failure and eye disease programs were not checked within the search budget. The old-mouse study did not report lifespan.
